Entertainment.title: Oasis 2027: Knebworth return confirmed plus Manchester and Glasgow gigs
Entertainment.text:
After weeks of posting teasers on social media and underneath the Manchester sky, Oasis have confirmed a second leg of their smash hit reunion tour for summer 2027.

The band will return to the scene of their legendary 1996 gigs at Knebworth House to play four nights at the 125,000-capacity venue in September next year.

They will also play a 11-night residency at the home of their beloved Manchester City in June, after kicking off the tour with five gigs at Glasgow's Celtic Park in May.

The announcement dropped on Monday afternoon alongside a new trailer, external and a photograph of frontmen Liam and Noel Gallagher. "Start the celebrations!", read a message on the band's social media.

"After a period of reflection, 'The Most Damaging Pop Cultural Force In Recent British History' has declared itself fit for purpose and will once again return to lift the spirits of the people.

"Come witness the fitness. It shall be a sight to behold."

Oasis will return to Slane Castle in County Meath, Ireland, for two dates in September, after performances across Europe in July and in the US in August.

Sharing the trailer on his own personal X account, Liam, 53, commented: "Spiritual."

The now confirmed 38-date tour marks the next phase of Oasis's comeback following their acclaimed 2025 live reunion, which made an estimated £300 million at the box office.

A new ticket registration process, similar to that used for Glastonbury Festival, has been launched in a bid to avoid the noise and confusion of last time around.

The registration period began on Monday with the announcement, on the band's website, and closes at 16:00 BST on Thursday 17 September.

In the UK, tickets will then go on sale across Friday 25, Saturday 26 and Sunday 27 September.

The band says standard ticket prices will be fixed and range between £71.50 and £266.60.

The special guest will be Richard Ashcroft again for all dates.

Singer-songwriter Noel recently teased the band's 2027 return - after a year off - telling TalkSport, external: "There must be something happening."

The band then posted a series of cryptic videos on their official social media channels appearing to tease gigs across the UK and Europe.

This was followed by a drone display outside the Etihad Stadium last week, pointing to Monday's announcement, as well as something similar in Rome and gig posters on the Paris Metro.

Manchester City fans the Gallaghers played a string of shows together at the Etihad Stadium in 2005, almost a decade after two famous nights at their team's old ground, Maine Road, were caught on camera for a concert film titled There and Then.

A few months after Maine Road, the band played to 250,000 fans on the grounds of Knebworth House in Hertfordshire over two nights in August 1996 - shows that are regarded as Britpop's crowning moment.

More than 4% of the UK population applied for tickets to see the Gallaghers perform, alongside the likes of the Charlatans, Manic Street Preachers, The Prodigy and Chemical Brothers.

Speaking at the premiere of a Knebworth documentary film in 2021, Noel said Oasis had had "no fear" about the magnitude of the shows, adding that if they were to do it again now they would be "petrified".

The band's 2025 comeback got off to a shaky start before an E minor chord was even strummed, with fans criticising the ticket sales process after being asked to queue for hours, with some finding themselves having to pay hundreds of pounds more than they expected.

The fiasco triggered a UK government response. Following an investigation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), Ticketmaster agreed to several voluntary changes, external, including telling fans 24 hours in advance if a tiered pricing system is in use and giving clearer information about ticket prices while people wait in the queue, as well as not using misleading ticket labels.

Demand and expectation were huge among fans, old and new. But the band delivered, with the BBC's review saying they hadn't sounded so good since the 1990s.

Mid-way through the world tour, Noel told TalkSport that he and his bandmates had been "blown away" by the response to their return after 16 years away.

Last week, another emotional documentary chronicling the tour - and featuring the reconciled brothers' first joint interview since their acrimonious split in 2009 - was released in UK cinemas, following its premiere in Venice.

In it, Noel confirms the band is "not a power struggle any more".

On Monday, following the announcement, he told the same radio station, external that booking part two of the comeback tour had been a no-brainer.

"We were having such a great time that, why wouldn't you?" said the musician, who will turn 60 on the day of the final Celtic Park concert.

He confirmed there would be no new Oasis music off the back of the tour.

Renewed interest in Oasis recently saw their second album (What's The Story) Morning Glory? officially overtake the biggest-selling album by their heroes The Beatles in the list of the UK's most popular albums of all-time.

And Wonderwall, from that album, became a bittersweet England World Cup anthem this summer.

Excitement for Knebworth has been growing for years - ever since it was rumoured to be on the itinerary for Oasis's 2025 tour.

Earlier this summer, it emerged that the band's promoters had applied for an events licence that would cover the Knebworth gigs.

Other big artists to have performed at the grounds of the listed country house venue include Led Zeppelin, Queen, Sir Paul McCartney, Metallica and, in 2022, Liam Gallagher as a solo act.

Oasis made history over two nights in 1996, but in 2003, Robbie Williams beat their combined attendance record by playing three consecutive nights, drawing a total crowd of 375,000 people.

That record now looks set to be broken again.

"This is history", as Noel once put it, now repeating itself 30 years on.

Entertainment.title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour after 'Free Palestine' speech
Entertainment.text:
Rapper Macklemore has been dropped from Ed Sheeran's US tour after making pro-Palestinian comments on stage earlier this month.

The artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - had been the opening act for Sheeran's Loop tour, but was criticised by Jewish groups after saying "Free Palestine" at two concerts and making political speeches.

Macklemore stood by his comments on Monday, confirming that he had been cut from the tour and writing in a statement that the real victims are the Palestinian people in Gaza.

Ed Sheeran has not yet commented, and who will replace Macklemore for the rest of the tour is unknown.

The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore, a long-time pro-Palestine activist, performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.

After that performance, the campaign group StopAntisemitism criticised the rapper, saying "Jewish fans bought tickets to see Ed Sheeran sing... not to be ambushed by Macklemore's anti-Israel propaganda."

The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience.

"Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.

Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

But the backlash against Macklemore only grew louder, and included a petition by the Israeli-American Council urging Sheeran to remove him from the tour.

"This was an Ed Sheeran concert - not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event," the council said, adding that the rapper used "biased messaging and disputed claims."

In his statement on Instagram, which was nearly 1,000 words long, Macklemore said that after a week of "difficult conversations" with Sheeran, that ultimately ended "in a place of fundamental disagreement", he was dropped from the lineup.

Tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone magazine that it had been told by venues that they would not allow Macklemore to perform, "which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans."

American businessman Robert Kraft, who owns the Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts, said he banned Macklemore because the venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric".

"I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said.

In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran was in, but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance.

"Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote.

He also addressed the accusations of antisemitism, writing that "one of the most effective ways to enforce silence has been to weaponize the accusation of antisemitism".

Macklemore added: "When criticizing Israel, opposing Zionism or saying "Free Palestine" gets conflated with hatred of Jewish people, it doesn't protect Jewish people. It protects Israel from accountability."

But he emphasised that even though he only did two shows on the tour, if his words succeeded in "turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on."

Entertainment.title: Bob Mackie: Legendary costume designer dies aged 87
Entertainment.text:
Bob Mackie, who designed dazzling costumes for stars including Cher, Tina Turner, Dolly Parton and Elton John has died, aged 87.

The US fashion designer, known as the "Sultan of Sequins" for his sparkling creations, won a Tony Award, nine Emmys and received three Oscar nominations during his career.

"It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr Bob Mackie passed away today," a statement on his Instagram account announced on Monday.

"He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do," it added. "His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world."

Mackie was particularly influential in Cher's career and designed her iconic Mohawk outfit, which she wore to the Oscars in 1986. It became known as her "revenge" outfit, because she wasn't nominated for anything.

The showgirl-inspired costume featured a plumed mohawk headdress and showed Cher's bare midriff - a very new, and very shocking look at the time.

The costume has gone down in fashion history as one of the most outrageous and extravagant ever to appear at the awards.

"I didn't get nominated for a movie that everyone thought I would actually win for [Mask] - so was dressing that night for a kind of revenge," Cher explained in the 2024 documentary Bob Mackie: Naked Illusion.

Mackie told the BBC in 2010 that when Cher started out she "looked like no-one else in the entertainment business at the time".

"Everybody just went crazy over this woman as she could wear anything," he added.

Cher was widely reported to be the first woman to show her belly button on US television - and Mackie's designs were pivotal to that.

Mackie was also the creative genius behind several of Sir Elton John's costumes, including his now-iconic Dodgers baseball outfit - bedazzled of course - that he wore during his performances at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles in 1975.

"Every time I put something on that Bob made, I felt very, very special," Sir John wrote on Instagram. "His costumes were works of art, and he will go down as one of the most legendary designers ever in Hollywood."

Singer Pink wore many of his designs over the years. Sharing several of the outfits she wore on stage during her Funhouse tour in 2009, she wrote "I was so lucky to be dressed by him for so long. He was loving, wickedly funny and an absolute genius."

"There are going to be some fabulously dressed angels."

Mackie was still designing up until recently - Sabrina Carpenter wore one of his designs at the MTV Video Music Awards last year.

He also designed the dress Miley Cyrus wore during her performance at the 2024 Grammy Awards. She won a Grammy that year for her break-up anthem, Flowers - perhaps it was her own version of a "revenge" dress.

Entertainment.title: ‘I’m fearless. I was in a boys’ rugby team’: Slow Horses’ Aimee-Ffion Edwards on playing a cocaine-snorting spy
Entertainment.text:
There was a moment, just before Aimee-Ffion Edwards jumped off a nightclub balcony in Slow Horses, when she had to lie to herself about what she was about to do. “It was quite hard,” says the actor. “You basically tell yourself, ‘You’re not jumping.’ Obviously, you know you’re harnessed in, but you’re also going, ‘This is mad! This is mad! This is mad!’”

She laughs. “I couldn’t feel my fingers for a second. I was like, ‘Huwwaah!’” She sucks in her breath, then says: “But there were 200 people stood there watching. You’re like, ‘Well, I gotta do it.’”

In the scene that we see, though, Shirley Dander – the tough, traumatised, cocaine-snorting MI5 agent Edwards plays – does not hesitate, leaping from the balcony to land on a suspect. That collision (on a stuntman) was no soft landing either and, at 38, Edwards knew she’d feel it the next day. And yet she jumped off the balcony “five or six times” during filming. “I played rugby in a boys’ team,” she explains, “and I think I have a fearlessness that comes from that. It’s quite instinctive.”

Edwards is wearing an elegant sleeveless blouse, smart navy trousers and gold hoop earrings. She does not, as she sits there sipping a flat white in London’s Soho Hotel, look much like a rugby player. Yet, with some pride, she reveals that her childhood dream was to play rugby for Wales, where she was born and raised. “That was all I cared about. And I did! I played one match for Wales. Then I was like, ‘I’ve done that. I think I’m going to do some acting.’”

Edwards, a fluent Welsh speaker, still lives in Newport. She had a paper round there until she was 19 and grew up the middle child of five. “I have a strong sense of being part of a pack,” she says. The actor regularly commutes to London (“it’s so close – an hour and 35 minutes on a good train”) and finds it refreshing to be able to play a British spy with her authentic Welsh accent, pleased Shirley’s Welshness is not a talking point in the hit show.

“Nobody ever mentions it,” she says. “And I think that’s really important. It’s good to normalise it. We hear northern and other accents all the time, but Welsh accents have been underrepresented.” Except, she adds, in comedy roles. “Like there’s a novelty aspect to being Welsh – like it’s some sort of kooky thing. It’s really not.”

Before Slow Horses, which follows a ragtag bunch of reject MI5 agents who are presumed to be inept despite usually saving the day, Edwards had to fake a Brummie accent as the opportunistic criminal Esme Shelby in Peaky Blinders, and adopt a southern one as manipulative Elizabeth Barton, the “Holy Maid of Kent” in Wolf Hall.

But as Shirley, and especially as Richard Burton’s older sister Cis in the 2025 film Mr Burton, she has increasingly been able to lean into her Welsh identity. And now she is voicing Princess Leia in the first-ever Welsh language-dub of 1977 blockbuster Star Wars. Due to be broadcast in Wales on Christmas Day, its Han Solo will be voiced by Matthew Rhys. So is she a fan? “Oh my God, I was pinching myself. That was so surreal, being in a booth, watching the film and lip-syncing I was going, ‘I don’t know how I got here, but I’m here – and I’m here for it.’ It was amazing. And it’s brilliant the Welsh language dub is happening. I’d be excited even if I wasn’t in it.”

In season six of Slow Horses, about to launch on Apple TV, Shirley’s anger and grief about the death of her colleague Marcus, played by Kadiff Kirwan, keeps bubbling to the surface. This grief is, to some extent, genuine: “I found it really hard when Marcus died, especially coming in for season five, because it was quite a lonely experience.”

She and Kirwan were “partners in crime”, she says. “That unique relationship between Shirley and Marcus – it was purely platonic, but with a lot of love, a lot of frustration, a lot of projecting each other’s nonsense back at each other.” At the same time, his death has helped her to develop Shirley’s character emotionally. “There’s so much to play.”

As a strong, dangerous woman whose physical bravery and moral courage is undermined by her emotional cowardice, explosive temper and penchant for violence, Shirley is “liberating” to play. “I love that she’s scrappy,” says Edwards. “There’s so much negative energy in her and she doesn’t know what to do with it. She can’t communicate it properly.”

Edwards – whose first major role was as Sketch, the stalker in teen drama Skins – looks for contradictions in the women she plays, which may explain why she is so good at humanising liars, criminals and sneaks. “I’m fascinated by people’s strengths,” she says, “and the mechanisms we have to protect ourselves when we feel vulnerable.” Shirley, she says, gives off a “stench” of “Try it – come and get it” when she walks into a room. “But I understand why she is like she is. I keep trying to pick at those threads, to expose them a little bit.”

Gary Oldman, who plays the chain-smoking, whisky-drinking, rarely washing boss Jackson Lamb, is the joker of the cast. “He loves making people laugh. He’s always got an anecdote, a tale to tell. He’s very silly and funny – a fun father figure.”

In her spare time, Edwards exercises a lot, mainly swimming and running, because team sports are a problem. “The nature of this work means you can’t commit,” she says, adding that she also enjoys making furniture in her garage. If she ever gave up acting and working far from home, she’d like to get a dog and become a carpenter. “I love making things with wood.”

Social media doesn’t interest her much. “I’m here for YouTube videos about carpentry, but I don’t know why anyone would ever be interested in what I had for breakfast.” She prefers to keep her personal life private, to protect her family and those she loves. And perhaps as a result, even though strangers often smile at her like they know her, they rarely identify who she is, even in Newport. “They think we went to school together or I work in the corner shop, rather than know me off the telly.”

This suits her. No actor, she says, ever regrets someone appreciating their work. “If they do, they should quit.” But she feels lucky she gets to live “a normal life” in her home town, where no one bothers her. “I’ll tell you what my biggest achievement is: so many people messaged me one day, because I was once an answer on Pointless.”

The question on the TV quizshow was: name a famous Edwards. “Which is ironic, because nobody knew who I was.” She beams. “What a contradiction.”

Entertainment.title: No Big Deal review – is this how AI ends humanity … with a sitcom so bad it bores you to death?
Entertainment.text:
As you will no doubt be aware, one Anthropic researcher claimed there is a greater than one in 10 chance that AI will end all of humanity as we know it within the next decade. However, now that I’ve given it some thought, I think this statistic might actually be a little conservative. This is because I have just watched an episode of a sitcom created by AI, and if I ever have to do it again I’m genuinely going to die of boredom.

The show is No Big Deal, and it premiered on YouTube on Friday. I was apparently only the 376th person to watch it. This is by no means a recommendation that you become the 377th, more a warning to avoid it if your algorithm ever decides it hates you enough to suggest this.

No Big Deal bills itself as “The Office meets Dragons’ Den”, in that it is a workplace comedy about a group of angel investors who have to listen to various product pitches. In the first episode, the products include a toilet that analyses your poo and a sofa you can have sex on. The investors are nightmarish waxworks who speak with all the nuance and cadence of a satnav telling you that you just missed a turning.

If you’ve watched any AI-generated content recently, you’ll know the faults it has, and they are all present here. Shot-to-shot continuity is essentially nonexistent, with characters changing positions every time the camera cuts to a new angle. Background noise either is or isn’t there, seemingly on a whim. The characters – who all fitfully look enough like real-life actors to make the whole thing seem icky and exploitative – move around with not a trace of life behind their eyes. It remains completely impossible to care about anyone once you know they’ve been made by AI.

Perhaps the most depressing thing about No Big Deal is the fact that it was purportedly written by a human. Although all the characters, locations and scenes were churned out by a machine, the show was apparently written by Andrew Dickinson. Dickinson, once himself an angel investor, originally intended for the show to be made as a traditional television production. When he realised that this would be slow and expensive, he turned to AI.

To some degree, this makes sense. It is extraordinarily hard to get a television programme on the air. You can spend years grinding away on an idea, only to see it wither up and die when none of the eight commissioners currently working like the sound of it. Wouldn’t it be better to just seize control of the means of production and make the AI version?

On this evidence, absolutely not. This is not a funny show. It’s one-note and bawdy, and none of the jokes land. It seems as though, by rushing straight to AI, Dickinson has bypassed the development process that actually makes something good. You could cast the greatest human actors of their generation to perform this script and it would still be unwatchable.

Then again, even if by some miracle Dickinson had written the most hilarious sitcom of all time, it still would have turned to ash the moment he let it loose on these AI abominations. I really cannot overstate how terrible this thing is to look at. While the technology has improved to an extent that, should you pause a scene at just the right moment, the characters are photorealistic, there’s something truly deathly about watching them move.

Their lips don’t line up with dialogue. There’s a creepy smoothness to their movements. Sometimes, when they don’t have anything to do in a scene, they just sit there completely still like a powered-down robot. Their voices bark on monotonously like Siri reading out a pasta recipe. Even something as simple as a fist shake (a fist shake! In a sitcom! In 2026!) gets mauled beyond all recognition here, causing the shaker to judder and glitch as if they just stepped on an uninsulated wire.

The most tragic thing of all is that nobody involved can see that this is just a stepping stone to the endgame. Dickinson thinks he can get away without human actors or crew, but we are a nanosecond away from the technology deciding that it doesn’t need human writers, either. By capitulating even a jot to AI-created content, all Dickinson is doing is nudging himself further towards extinction.

And me, too, because if this is the future of entertainment then I’d rather die than write about it. If we really do only have a decade left, every second should be precious. Please don’t spend any of it watching crap like this.

Entertainment.title: ‘Every magazine cover needs to seduce’: designers pick their favourites
Entertainment.text:
‘We need to rethink what a successful magazine looks like,” says Steve Watson, founder of the subscription magazine club Stack. “It doesn’t make sense to compare the magazines of today to those of the 1960s when many people still didn’t have colour televisions. Print magazines are no longer the best way of reaching lots of people quickly and cheaply but they are still really great at engaging deeply with readers, providing an opportunity to slow down and absorb information. They provide us with an alternative way of seeing the world.”

Watson, along with a group of editors, publishers, designers, historians and academics, will be discussing the varying roles and functions that magazines have played over the years during a one-day event at the forthcoming London design festival. In contrast to the doom and gloom we often hear about the print industry, he remains upbeat about the humble mag’s future. “The truth is there are brilliant new magazines launching all the time,” he says.

And with every new title comes new opportunities for bold, innovative and eye-popping cover design. Here, industry experts – including many taking part in the London design festival event – pick out their favourite magazine cover designs and tell us why they find them so enduring …

Blast, issue 1, 1914

Scott King, ex-art director for i-D magazine and former creative director for Sleazenation

Blast was published a month before Britain entered the first world war. It was an anti-petit-bourgeois rant against the professional classes. It features lines such as “Curse abysmal inexcusable middle class” and “The britannic aesthete – cream of the snobbish earth”. It was – for want of a less gratuitous expression, given when it was published – a call to arms. It was punk 60 years before punk was invented. In fact, Blast often reads exactly like a Fall song [the band’s singer Mark E Smith was a huge fan], with the artist and editor Wyndham Lewis piecing together phrases into a collage of barely focused loathing: “Blast the amateur, sciolast, art-pimp, journalist, self man, no-organ man.”

S&M Sniper, issue 5, 1984

Meara Sharma, senior editor of Elastic

This is a fetish magazine but it does what I think every magazine cover needs to do: seduce. It’s luring a reader in, tickling the senses, giving a flavour of what’s inside, but also tantalising whoever’s passing by. This does a great job of fulfilling that mandate of seduction. The art itself is this incredible photorealistic airbrushed painting by Yosuke Onishi, an amazing Japanese artist who featured in every issue. So the artist gets to play, but you get this lovely consistency and distinct look, and it becomes unmistakably that magazine. It’s so lush, visceral and delicious. The lips are dripping and they feel like they’re bursting out of the page.

Colors, issue 90, 2014

Steve Watson, founder of Stack magazines

This is the last issue of Colors ever published and it was edited by Patrick Waterhouse, who I think is a genius. This was the year of the World Cup in Brazil, so they did a survival guide to football but they took a completely different view. There’s stuff in here about refugee and amputee teams and artists who change the shape of the football pitch to explore what it would do to the game. It’s full of of nice little symmetries and links: it’s issue 90 and a football match is 90 minutes long, and the cover has got this gold foil on it that references football cards. It’s loads of fun, but also really clever.

Cosmopolitan debut UK issue, 1972

Dr Sharon Maxwell Magnus, media historian and principal lecturer in mass communications at the University of Hertfordshire

Cosmopolitan was different from anything that went before it. Other women’s magazines in the UK, at the time, focused on domestic life, family, cooking, recipes, and were very homely. This was for women not bound by marriage and children, and who can, and are, having sex before or outside marriages. The cover is a brilliant partnership between design and words. It’s daring but not so daring that newsagents aren’t going to stock it. It was a revolutionary moment for the magazine industry and it sold 350,000 copies by lunchtime on its first day.

Life magazine: Faces of the American Dead in Vietnam, 1969

Jaap Biemans, art director at Volkskrant magazine

This cover is like a slap in the face. You have the image of a face, just like you see on thousands of covers, but when you read the headline you get goosebumps everywhere. It’s the maximum of emotion with minimal elements. It’s a great execution by cropping the face and, design-wise, it’s the most simple cover you can make but it’s got such an impact. When you look at normal covers about war, you see heroic poses, grieving people, flags, explosions, battlefields. But on this one, you don’t see any of that, but it fires into your mind and heart like an arrow.

Cornhill, December 1865

Tony Quinn, magazine historian and founder of Magforum

The people behind this cover were all working at the top of their trade. It was edited by William Makepeace Thackeray and engraved by WJ Linton, while designer Godfrey Sykes was working at the time on the architectural decoration for the V&A Museum. Cornhill was named after a street that had a market where they brought in agricultural products, so Sykes interprets Cornhill via the manufacturing of corn: each roundel shows a stage of making it. Everything about this cover has a story behind it. It also changed the way that names were invented for magazines – within about 40 years there were dozens of magazines named after streets in London, from Pall Mall to the Strand.

Bloomberg Businessweek, 2 May, 2016

Alice Sherwin and Harry Bennett, founders of Studio Ground Floor

Designer Tracy Ma’s run for Bloomberg Businessweek was unbelievable – as her work continues to be. For us, this is a particular standout, because it both embodies her editorial approach to the periodical and taps into something we love in design: everyday visual language. Typographically, systematically and spatially, Tracy draws on familiar visual cues, the design that comes to exist without designer’s involvement, and subverts them. That way, people are drawn in and then shown something surprisingly new. In this case, it’s super self-aware. Kitsch and boring. It’s sublime design and a capsule for the time, helping its audience better understand the issue at hand through creative choices.

New York magazine, Lindsay Lohan as Marilyn Monroe, 2008

Charlie Baker, editor of the Fence

I was 19, living in New York, and remember being struck by this. I think this was the last era when you could do a cover that would be a little bit daring, bold, and put it out into the ecosystem as a way of getting readers to buy it. It was like a last great show of what covers can do. I think it’s good for tasteful erotic things to be in mainstream culture but I don’t think you could do something like that now.

Frieze, issue 134, 2010

Frith Kerr, art director at Studio Frith

I love this. It’s an instinctive, joyful response to something poetic made from the very ordinary: a sock, a foot and a logotype. The image is so concise that the magazine becomes an artwork – an egalitarian one that you can afford. Art should not only be for the super-rich. The scale is important, as is the sharp yellow of the logotype. The graphic simplicity poses a question. It is a visual idea. Questions are much more potent than answers as they engage and form relationships. Visual communication is all about creating relationships. A good magazine cover, like this, will instantly do that.

Interview magazine, Lana Del Rey, 2023

Jeremy Leslie, founder of magCulture

This cover really struck a chord. The photoshoot by Nadia Lee Cohen is timeless, this could have been the 1950s or 70s. It’s a fabulous portrait of a woman that was really of that moment. It sold out and became hugely in demand. I visit universities for talks and there’s a box of magazines I take with me and my copy of that went missing at one. It’s easy to go back and find classic covers from, say, the 1960s but that was a different time. It’s interesting seeing how today a cover can still punch above its weight and deliver something that’s an iconic cultural moment.

Entertainment.title: ‘She went to her studio every day and no one was allowed near it’: the glorious nature paintings of Yasmin David
Entertainment.text:
When Clio David was growing up, her mother’s studio was off-limits. The wooden outbuilding where her mother, Yasmin, went to paint was in the apple orchards that surrounded her childhood home in south Devon. It had once been a dormitory for the students of Dartington Hall, a progressive school where Clio’s father taught during the 1960s.

“It was somewhere she went every day to paint and work, and no one was allowed near it,” says Clio. “The walls of our house were covered in her paintings, but the studio was a private place.”

Yasmin’s own family had celebrated and nurtured creativity. Her mother, Lorna, was one of the Garman siblings, a free-spirited family whose friendships and love affairs connected everyone from Peggy Guggenheim to Vita Sackville-West. Lorna married Ernest Wishart, a wealthy communist who co-founded socialist publishing house Lawrence & Wishart, but she was also Lucian Freud’s lover and the subject of a number of his paintings before the painter met and married Lorna’s niece, Kitty. When she was 19, Yasmin discovered that her biological father was writer Laurie Lee. He dedicated his 1944 book of poetry, The Sun My Monument, to her mother and to “Y”. Yasmin found out that her name was chosen because a capital letter Y resembles two conjoined Ls – to symbolise Laurie and Lorna’s relationship.

But Yasmin quit London and art school at 23, moving to rural Devon with her husband Julian David, who became a Jungian analyst. She lived on Luscombe farm for much of the rest of her life, and the full extent of her painting talent was only discovered after her death. Clio was going through her mother’s possessions, and opened a cupboard to find more than 200 canvases and 550 works on paper neatly stacked inside – luminous, brooding pictures of the area’s moorland, woods and rivers, with the wild landscape lit by spectral sunlight. There was also a wealth of poetry, nature writing and touching letters from Yasmin’s father.

A selection of these pieces were shown alongside the paintings in a memorial show at the New Art Gallery Walsall in 2021. The gallery had been built by Lorna’s sister, Kathleen Garman, to showcase work by her husband, sculptor Jacob Epstein.

This month, Yasmin’s work is in a new solo show that focuses on her contribution to British landscape painting. The Nature of Light, featuring more than 40 works on canvas alongside drawings, sketches, notebooks and photographs, is at the Thelma Hulbert Gallery in Honiton, about 40 miles from Yasmin’s home in Luscombe.

Curator Gemma Girvan says: “Presenting Yasmin’s works here brings them full circle, reconnecting them to the place which inspired them. Yasmin lived and worked on the edge of Dartmoor and many of the landscapes she painted will be instantly recognisable to our local audiences. We hope this exhibition will encourage wider debate about the many talented female artists whose work remains under-recognised including our gallery’s namesake, Thelma Hulbert.”

Art historian Sophie Hatchwell, who is giving a talk on Yasmin’s work during the run of the show, says that it “sits in comparison with that of Joan Eardley, Barbara Delaney and Gillian Ayres. It offers a way into thinking about the British landscape outside the traditional patriarchal framework as a territory to be conquered.”

The British art world, confronting its long history of institutional bias and sexism, is now reconsidering the importance of female art inspired by nature. The Courtauld gallery in London ran the exhibition A View of One’s Own: Landscapes by British Women Artists this spring, and artists as disparate as Cuban sculptor Ana Mendieta and British printmaker Angie Lewin have major shows either on or scheduled.

Clio David, a documentary film-maker based in London, is now sharing her mother’s work with academics at the Courtauld Institute to ensure Yasmin’s contribution to the landscape genre is recognised. “She was one of the few women working in landscape during the latter part of the 20th century, and I want to place her archive within that period of art history.”

Yasmin’s art is unique, but her background undeniably is, too. And raising the profile of her work would also change the picture of a family where typically women supported the men in their creative endeavours. Clio is all too aware of this: “I want to show her work as her family history is largely dominated by male artists and writers – Laurie Lee, Lucian Freud, Jacob Epstein, Roy Campbell, Michael Wishart. She was a female artist from a very well-connected family, but working outside the art establishment on a farm in the middle of the countryside, about as far from the Colony Rooms as you could get. I want her work as an artist to be recognised and celebrated.”

Entertainment.title: No one could stand in the way of this juggernaut! The biggest shocks from the Emmy awards
Entertainment.text:
To tell the story of how Hacks performed at last night’s Emmys, you have to acknowledge both its incredible success and its terrible failure. The first is undeniable. Last night, Jean Smart won lead actress in a comedy series yet again. This meant that every time Hacks brought out a new season, Smart won the same award for it. This makes her the first woman to ever win an Emmy for every season of a programme’s run. It’s a history-making achievement, and thoroughly well earned.

The flipside of that, however, is that this is all Hacks won last night. One Emmy is better than many shows can even hope to dream of, but the reality is that Hacks swaggered into the Emmys with a record 24 nominations – the most ever for a comedy in a single year – and had the momentum of a huge farewell narrative behind it. But it only ended up winning one for Jean Smart and a Creative Arts Emmy for picture editing. In other words, last night Hacks lost 22 Emmys.

This isn’t a complete surprise. My long-held theory about Hacks is that while lots of people enjoyed it, it was always a bit of a protest vote. The show’s big year – 2024, when it finally won outstanding comedy series – came when the industry was tying itself in knots trying to decide whether The Bear should qualify as a comedy or not. Hacks was the biggest immediately identifiable comedy in a weak field at the time, so that’s where the votes went. In other words, it primarily won because nobody wanted The Bear to win.

Since then, shows that are easier to love came along. Seth Rogen’s The Studio – same subject matter but more pointed, more technically ambitious and funnier – swept the board last year, and this time around it was the turn of Widow’s Bay. Did Hacks deserve better? Perhaps. In its final season, Hannah Einbinder was allowed to play more notes than she did in the year that she won. Either way, all involved have to be fairly disappointed this morning.

Then again, who’d stand in the way of a juggernaut like Widow’s Bay? A genuinely funny, genuinely scary comedy-horror, Widow’s Bay won a grand total of 14 Emmys this year. There are seven comedy awards presented during the televised ceremony, and Widow’s Bay won six of them; outstanding comedy series, lead actor in a comedy, supporting actor in a comedy, supporting actress in a comedy, writing for a comedy and directing for a comedy. Obviously Jean Smart won the seventh for Hacks, but it’s worth pointing out that Widow’s Bay didn’t field a nominee in that category.

None of this will come as a surprise if you’ve actually seen the show. However, one surprise might come in the form of Matthew Rhys. His win for Widow’s Bay was never in question – in one episode he pulled a face of surprise that probably could have won an Emmy by itself – but the interesting thing is that he also won lead actor in a limited or anthology series or movie for The Beast in Me.

That was a much harder fought category, and the frontrunner was always thought to be Oscar Isaac for the second season of Beef. One working theory here is that his work on Widow’s Bay was so extraordinary that the affection for him spilled over into an entirely different show. Either way, Rhys has now become the first actor to win lead actor Emmys in comedy, drama and limited series.

Elsewhere there were plenty of smaller upsets. Allison Janney winning best supporting actress in a drama for The Diplomat certainly came as a shock, especially since The Pitt’s Katherine LaNasa had such a powerhouse year. Same for Sally Field, who won an award for Remarkably Bright Creatures ahead of Carey Mulligan, who was tremendous in Beef. Stephen Root’s win for Widow’s Bay meant that Harrison Ford remains Emmyless, which is extraordinary given both Ford’s age and the Emmy predilection for handing awards to the most famous people who turn up on the night.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Denmark says Russian warship fired flares at military helicopter
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.

The Danish government has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which it said happened during a "routine" monitoring operation on Monday.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the Russian action "reckless" and said it was designed to "intimidate and divide".

Russia said it would "thoroughly investigate" the incident but accused Danish helicopters of making "dangerous manoeuvres" near Russian warships.

It came on the same day that Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high amid Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In a statement detailing the incident in the Baltic Sea, the Danish armed forces said: "One of the air force's Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser."

Of the two flares fired at the helicopter, one passed close to it, the statement added.

The Danish foreign ministry described the incident as "completely unacceptable".

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen accused Russia of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour", adding: "That is something we cannot accept."

In a statement, Russian ambassador Vladimir Barbin said Moscow would "thoroughly investigate all the circumstances of the incident" but accused the Danish helicopter of carrying out "provocative actions".

Barbin said this was "not the first time that Danish Air Force helicopters have carried out dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships".

He said he had complained about a similar incident last year, adding that the latest event showed that "communication problems lie not with the Russian Navy's vessels, but with the Danish side".

Russia's behaviour was "reckless and dangerous," the President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen said in a post on social media.

This incident – together with the drone over Lithuania – was "part of a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe", she added.

Danish Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters no attempt to make contact with helicopters had been made by the frigate's crew.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Reform's Dan Thomas resigns as Wales leader after being arrested
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Reform UK's Dan Thomas has quit as the party's Welsh leader, after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour on Sunday.

Gwent Police said a 45-year-old man from Aberbargoed, in Caerphilly was bailed pending further enquiries.

In a statement issued by his party, Thomas said he was "standing down" from his position due to personal reasons. He said he had been "released without charge".

Thomas was appointed Welsh party leader by Nigel Farage in February.

Thomas said: "I stress that I have done nothing wrong, but I do not want the coming headlines to be a distraction from the fantastic work our Senedd team is doing in holding this government to account."

Thomas did not take part in First Minister's Questions earlier today.

Thomas said: "It has been the honour of my life to have been the leader of Reform Wales and see this party go from zero to 34 elected members and become the largest opposition group in Welsh history.

"With deep regret, I am now standing down from this position due to personal reasons.

"Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge."

He added: "I will continue to serve my constituents in Casnewydd Islwyn and will fully back whoever the group selects as its next leader."

Gwent Police said: "On Sunday 13 September a 45-year-old man, from the Aberbargoed area, was arrested on suspicion of assault and engaging in controlling/coercive behaviour.

"He has been bailed pending further enquiries."

The former Conservative councillor grew up in Blackwood, in the south Wales valleys.

He led Barnet Council from 2019 until 2022 before defecting to Reform in June 2025.

He later quit as a councillor for Finchley Church End after returning to his home country with his family.

Thomas told a conference earlier this year that he had been "born and raised" in the Valleys before leaving for London to pursue a career in financial services.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Raheem Sterling admits dangerous driving on motorway before crash
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before he crashed a Lamborghini in May.

The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.

Sterling, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of 28 May.

Sterling has 82 England caps, the last of which was won at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

The former England winger pleaded guilty to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road before he crashed.

The court heard he strayed into the central reservation of the M3, exited at junction 4A, and veered off the A327, crashing into "roadside infrastructure" in a layby.

The crash caused "substantial" damage to his car and all four wheels, which prevented him from driving further, the court heard.

He was in possession of six canisters of nitrous oxide, a Class C drug.

Prosecutor Simon Jones said that between 7:45 and 8:52 police received a number of calls about dangerous driving on the two motorways.

When police arrived on the scene of the collision Sterling was in the passenger seat of the car with two nitrous oxide canisters on his lap, the court was told.

Witnesses described seeing a Lamborghini driver inhaling from a white balloon.

Fiona Jennings, who saw the vehicle on the M3 at 8:45, said she looked across and thought that an airbag had inflated, but then realised it was an inflated balloon.

She told police she saw "absolutely horrendous driving" as the Lamborghini swerved in and out of lanes.

"She had genuine concerns the driver might kill someone," Jones said.

Sterling complied with a road side breath test, which was negative, and a preliminary drug test, which indicated no cannabis or cocaine.

However, tests carried out at the Basingstoke police investigation centre deemed that he was impaired.

During the process he disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", Jones said.

A sample of blood could only be taken with his consent, which he did not give.

Sterling asked to obtain legal advice before making a decision, Mr Jones said, but in the police sergeant's view "he was deliberately failing to provide a clear answer".

In the police interview that followed, Sterling accepted he had been the driver, and provided "no comment" answers to the driving.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said there was no dispute that the case was a "top category" because of the "at times" serious impairment, though it would have been for short periods within the driving.

But the defence did not accept the damage to the car was serious, and said there was "confusion" over the failure to provide a specimen.

Hampshire Police previously said the charges followed a single-vehicle collision near the M3 southbound, near the Minley interchange.

The force said no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Ed Sheeran says it was 'not my decision' to drop Macklemore from tour
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Ed Sheeran has posted a long statement on Instagram, saying it was not his decision to drop Macklemore from his current US tour.

The US rapper - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - was ejected from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian statements at two dates in New Jersey.

His comments drew criticism from Jewish groups, after which some venues put pressure on the tour promoters to have him removed from the line-up.

In his statement, external, Sheeran said he had spoken with the venues "at length all week to try and build a bridge" - but the promoters, Messina Touring Group, had ultimately decided to remove Macklemore from the bill.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.

"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

The star also attempted to explain his decision not to become embroiled in political issues.

"I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care.

"Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way."

He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.

"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes.

"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: Peace.

"I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change."

The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which is dedicated to pro-Palestinian protestors at Columbia University and condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.

Some of the audience cheered - but there was almost immediate criticism online.

The Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour; while the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda - a claim that was amplified by the pop star Pink, who reposted it on Instagram.

The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience.

"Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.

Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Iran war has led to US munitions shortfalls, Pentagon inspector confirms
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The US defence department's inspector general says the war with Iran has led to "shortfalls" in munitions and a bottleneck in resupply, contradicting President Donald Trump who has repeatly denied the US is facing shortages.

Trump has claimed US munitions supplies are "virtually unlimited" and said reporting otherwise is "fake news".

But the independent watchdog said the US spent more than $22 billion on munitions from February through June, leading to "strategic inventory shortfalls".

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment about the discrepancy.

The new report provides a first-of-its-kind, independent glimpse into US weapons stockpiles, data that is typically classified.

Previous estimates have painted a dire picture of the US shortages.

Over the course of the war, US forces have expended vast quantities of both long-range ground attack systems and the air and missile defences used to intercept incoming Iranian attacks.

A late July estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, or CSIS, found that stocks of some interceptors - such as the Patriot missile and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD - were significantly depleted, in some cases by more than half.

The inspector general's report did not disclose exactly how many of the weapons remain.

It did, however, note the inventory shortfalls and reveal "industrial base bottlenecks" for munitions resupply.

The report added that the defence department is now working to "streamline procurement processes and production lead times" to address the shortages and "respond rapidly to a contingency".

Trump and other administration officials have sought to cast reports of shortages as false and "treasonous".

In a 4 August X post, for example, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth described news reporting on the shortages as "not true".

And in a lengthy Truth Social post on 3 September, Trump claimed that the US had "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition and is "stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen".

The watchdog's report also notes that equipment losses have totaled $3.7bn, with other $7.4bn in other expenditures. Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war from 28 Feb to 30 Jun.

Among the losses have been four F-15e fighter jets, a highly advanced F-35 Joint Strike Fighter and 30 MQ-9 drones destroyed in "various circumstances".

When US and Israeli strikes began, Trump repeatedly said that the conflict would be over within weeks.

More recently, he said the conflict might not end until "right after" the November midterm elections in the US.

Polls show that the war is unpopular among Americans.

One Reuters/Ipsos poll released in early September found that only 23% of Americans - and only half of Republicans - believe the US to be in a stronger position with Iran compared with before hostilities broke out.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Trump criticises Supreme Court after justices block mail-in ballot restrictions
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The US Supreme Court has rejected President Donald Trump's plan to restrict voting by mail before November's midterm elections, in a setback for the White House.

The justices upheld a federal judge's order that temporarily blocked the US Postal Service (USPS) from moving forwards with new requirements for postal ballots.

Trump called the decision a blow to his political party. "Republicans just got another bad decision from the United States Supreme Court," the president wrote on Truth Social.

One legal group said in response that the decision would prevent the USPS from "sowing chaos in our elections".

The ruling is unlikely to be the final word on the matter. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a conservative, agreed with the ruling, but indicated he might later rule in Trump's favour as litigation in the case continues.

Trump, who argued the rules would combat electoral fraud, signed an executive order in March that directed the USPS to deliver ballots only to voters on lists of citizens.

Legal challenges argued that the move violated states' constitutional rights to run elections.

Election officials from 24 Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia also warned that the proposed changes were not ready for implementation and could prevent ballots from reaching voters.

Meanwhile some Republican-led states, including Florida, Louisiana, and Montana, supported the president in court filings.

Justice Kavanaugh wrote in the opinion that there was "at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority". But he argued that "applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious".

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, also conservatives, dissented. They wrote that the challenge to Trump's order was a "Hail Mary pass" that was unlikely to be successful ultimately.

In a Truth Social post, Trump criticised the top court's Monday decision, as well as other key rulings against him such as striking down his executive order to limit birthright citizenship, and also a key element of his tariff policies.

"The Supreme Court has really let our Country down!" he wrote, alleging some justices were "totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America".

"These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," the president wrote.

About 30% of voters, mostly Democrats, cast postal ballots in the general election two years ago.

However, several states like Oregon, Washington, and Colorado rely heavily or entirely on mail ballots for their elections, requiring Republicans to use the system as well.

Seven Republican state election officials warned the justices, external that allowing significant changes to mail ballot rules so close to the midterm elections would "lead to mistakes, delays, and confusion".

Local election officials told the BBC this week they were proceeding as normal but had begun drafting contingency plans in case the court upended existing mail ballot procedures.

The rule changes would have resulted in "thousands of people disenfranchised" in Cherokee County, Georgia, its election director Anne Dover told the BBC. The heavily Republican county voted 69% for Trump in the 2024 election, in which about 10,000 of its residents voted by mail, according to Dover.

Monday's decision earned praise from legal groups who have challenged other aspects of the Trump agenda.

"Today's Supreme Court decision prevents the US Postal Service from sowing chaos in our elections," Trevor Potter, president of Campaign Legal Center, said in a statement.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has sought to restrict voting by mail. While he himself has voted by post, he has long claimed this method allows non-citizens to cast ballots and is prone to fraud.

In March's executive order, the president directed USPS to introduce unique barcodes on postal ballot envelopes.

State and local election officials would also be required to supply information to an online portal about voters who receive mail ballots.

Twenty-three states and Washington DC sued to stop Trump's order.

The postal workers' union also said clerks could not be trained in time for the election.

In court filings, the Trump administration maintained the new USPS rules were constitutional.

It said states "cannot choose to use the federal mails to carry out their elections but then insist that their election-related mail is somehow exempt from the Postal Service's rule-making authority, conferred by Congress".

Boston-based Judge Indira Talwani imposed an injunction on 4 September blocking Trump's order. She ruled that implementing the measures close to November's elections could disenfranchise voters.

Last week, a US appeals court refused to put Judge Talwani's order on hold.

On Sunday, another federal judge, Judge Carl Nichols, ruled against Trump's order.

Some states have already begun distributing mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress.

Some states that had not yet sent ballots had already printed their election materials, and changing their voting materials would have required starting the process anew.

"Hypothetically, if we did have to implement, it would have a huge impact, and it would be very costly. At this point, we already have our envelopes printed," Josh Zygielbaum, the Adams County, Colorado clerk and recorder, told the BBC the day before the Supreme Court ruled.

Colorado conducts its elections by mail, and Zygielbaum had been creating contingency plans in the event its voting system had been disrupted.

The Supreme Court decision is not the first setback on postal ballots for Trump.

In June, the justices ruled that states may count ballots postmarked by election day, rejecting the Trump administration's push to block votes being tallied when they are received after polls close.

Trump has previously made false claims that he lost the 2020 election owing to widespread electoral fraud.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Harry and Meghan change children's school over security concerns due to traffic
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have changed their children's school only days after they first started over security concerns about traffic during the school run.

The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.

It's understood that the security for the children meant travelling with another car, and that driving in convoy proved difficult in the busy school run traffic.

The checks on the route are believed to have initially taken place before term time, but with the school traffic it was deemed not safe enough.

A source close to the couple said: "The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family's security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements."

They added: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

It has also emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

The prince previously mounted an unsuccessful legal challenge over his police security when he was visiting from the US.

But the family's return to the UK has meant a different set of circumstances for their taxpayer-funded security, and last week the Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - met to discuss their case.

This committee, which includes representatives of the Home Office, the police and the Royal Household, seems ready to review potential dangers.

This means a so-called Risk Management Board will consider the threats against them and the level of police protection they might need - although no final decision on the outcome has been reached.

The review will include security for their children Archie, aged seven, and Lilibet, aged five, who started school earlier this month but, as first reported by HELLO! magazine, external, the children have switched schools because of a security issue.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Emmys remember Catherine O'Hara, Rob Reiner and Hayden Panettiere
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy delivered a poignant tribute to their late Home Alone and Schitt's Creek co-star Catherine O'Hara, at Monday's Emmy Awards in Los Angeles.

Culkin remembered her as "our mom", and "like a good mom, she always showed up when I asked her to".

US singer-songwriter Noah Kahan performed Bridge Over Troubled Water during the in memoriam segment on the night, before Jamie Lee Curtis paid an emotional tribute to the late actor and director Rob Reiner.

Heroes and Nashville star Hayden Panettiere, who died last month, was also remembered alongside other stars including Rocky Horror Show's Tim Curry and Dawson's Creek actor James Van Der Beek.

Emmy winner O'Hara, who died in January this year aged 71, was known for playing Culkin's frantic mother in the 1990s film franchise, as well as the eccentric Moira Rose - mum to Murphy and Levy's Alexis and Dan - in Schitt's Creek.

"You remember her as the forgetful mother, right?" said Culkin.

"There are all kinds of words I could use to describe Catherine. She was encouraging. She was warm. She was funny, but the word that I think of is mom... She was, she was my mom. She was our mom."

Referring to the plot of the Home Alone films, he joked: "She may have forgotten me... twice! But we will always remember her."

Murphy noted how, since her death, many people had quoted O'Hara's most memorable lines from her show back at her.

"These are only very few of the interactions I've been lucky enough to have that remind me how profoundly Catherine has impacted the world, and it's because she brought us joy," Murphy said.

O'Hara's final acting role, as movie executive Patty Leigh in Seth Rogen's satire The Studio, earned her an Emmy and a Golden Globe nomination.

Levy added: "Always say yes to any opportunity to revel in the presence of greatness."

The emotional moment, which featured a giant image of a smiling O'Hara as the backdrop, appeared to bring actors Martin Short and Steve Martin, sitting in the audience, to tears.

Reiner, who was killed along with his wife last year, received a posthumous Emmy last week for his guest appearance in The Bear.

A tearful Jamie Lee Curtis paid tribute to the director, writer and performer, who made films such as When Harry Met Sally, This is Spinal Tap, Stand By Me, Misery and A Few Good Men, calling him a "cherished legend" and "our beloved meathead".

The 48-year gap between Reiner's two most recent Emmy wins set a new record, beating his dad, Carl Reiner.

Curtis began her speech by first acknowledging the passing of Cheers co-creator James Burrows, who was also a good friend of Reiner's.

There were also warm words for Farrah Fawcett, who died in 2009.

Celebrating 50 years of Charlie's Angels, original stars Kate Jackson, Cheryl Ladd and Jaclyn Smith handed out the Emmy for best drama and paid tribute to their fellow Angel.

Jackson said Fawcett "was the shiniest angel of all, and she was loved by millions of people all over the world. And she still is today. And they'll never forget her and neither will we. And I'm sure you won't either."

Buffy the Vampire Slayer stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreana paid tribute to the co-stars they have lost recently, including Nicholas Brendon, Anthony Head and Michelle Trachtenberg.

Geller said: "David and I would like to acknowledge that it has been a tough two years for our beloved cast and crew, and we feel very lucky to have known and worked with such amazing people."

Elsewhere on the night, Remarkably Smart Creatures actress Sally Field, who starred in Steel Magnolias opposite Dolly Parton, led a tribute to the country music star, who died last month.

Field described Parton as "genuine, humble, supportive and blisteringly funny" as she introduced a special performance by country singer Reba McEntire.

"She was a humanitarian whose contribution has made a profound difference across our country," Field said of Parton, who won an Emmy herself in 2021.

"God bless you Dolly Parton my friend, I am not the only one on earth who will love you for ever and ever."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Petrol and diesel prices hit highest since 2022
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Petrol and diesel prices have both hit the highest levels since 2022 as the conflict in the Middle East continues to impact drivers' finances.

The average price of a litre of petrol now stands at 169.68p, according to the RAC motoring body, while diesel has risen to 191.68p.

The cost of filling up a vehicle is back to where it was after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago.

The US-Israel war with Iran has severely disrupted the production and transportation of oil across the region.

Motor fuel prices fell back when the US and Iran agreed in June to a framework deal to end the fighting but have started rising again as tensions resurface.

With the price of wholesale oil back above $100 a barrel, Simon Williams, head of policy at motoring organisation RAC, said "there's no end in sight to high pump prices" for drivers.

Crude oil is a key ingredient in petrol and diesel, which means that higher wholesale costs make filling up a car more expensive. The price of petrol and diesel is also heavily influenced by demand and refining capacity.

Analysts say every $10 (£7.44) per barrel increase in the oil price pushes up pump prices by roughly 7p a litre.

Since the war began, the price of a barrel of Brent crude – the global benchmark for wholesale oil prices – has been very volatile.

Generally speaking, news of further conflict drives the price up while hopes of an end to the war pushes the price down.

Before the conflict, Brent was about $70 a barrel, but the fighting saw it peak at above $120.

In early July, after the framework deal was signed, prices fell back to near the $70 a barrel mark.

When the peace talks collapsed, the price climbed back up again to above $100 a barrel. It fell back for a few weeks but is once again over the $100 mark after a fresh escalation in hostilities.

Just a few weeks ago in July, the average price of petrol was 150.59p per litre and diesel was 164.52p.

They have since rebounded. At 191.68p for a litre of diesel, the price is getting closer to the record high of 199.05p seen in June 2022.

Meanwhile, petrol has hit an average 169.68p a litre. It remains below a peak of 191.5p during the summer of 2022.

Williams said: "This takes the cost of filling up a 55-litre family car with unleaded to over £93 and diesel to more than £105."

Because transporting oil is a slow process, price movements in wholesale oil markets take about a fortnight to show at the pump.

Fuel retailers have denied accusations of price gouging during the conflict. The official markets regulator said it had "not seen evidence of retailers actively changing their pricing strategies to take advantage of the crisis".

A government scheme called Fuel Finder, external lets drivers compare the cost of fuel offered by petrol stations across the UK.

In May, the then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said a planned 5p increase in fuel duty due in September would be postponed until the end of December because of the conflict.

RAC has said there is "a very strong case" for leaving fuel duty at its current level, at least until the end of the Parliament.

The UK is heavily reliant on oil and gas imports, with the majority coming from the US and Norway.

The price of oil on the global market determines how much the UK pays for it.

Although the UK does get some oil from the North Sea, most of that is exported for refining elsewhere.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Israeli minister threatens to revoke filmmakers' citizenship over Gaza documentary
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Israel's culture minister has called for the Oscar-winning Israeli co-directors of Naza, a documentary that accuses the Israeli army of mass civilian killings in Gaza, to be stripped of their citizenship over "treason against the state".

Named for the Hebrew military acronym for collateral damage, the film speaks to 24 unidentified Israeli military and intelligence officers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used by the Israeli army to bombard Gaza in the war triggered by the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.

Since then, more than 73,000 Palestinians, including more than 20,000 children, have been killed in the campaign by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, figures considered reliable by the UN. About 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage during the Hamas attack.

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor say their 80-minute documentary "details the systems behind Israel's calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza" during the war, according to its official synopsis. One of the people interviewed says there was the approval for an attack to kill 500 people for "one human target", an allegation the IDF said was "completely false".

In a post on X, Culture Minister Miki Zohar said he had asked the authorities "to investigate how the materials were obtained, who is behind them, and whether in the process of obtaining or publishing them, actions were taken that amount to aiding the enemy during wartime".

In a letter addressed to Israel's Interior Ministry, he said: "The claims presented in the film are false and distorted, and I categorically reject the attempt to portray IDF soldiers and the State of Israel as perpetrators of intentional crimes." Zohar mentioned the country's Citizenship Law, saying it "allows for the revocation of citizenship due to a 'breach of allegiance to the State of Israel'". The measure, however, has rarely been applied.

There has been no immediate reaction from Abraham and Szor. The filmmakers won an Oscar last year for No Other Land, a documentary about violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Naza premiered last Thursday at the Venice Film Festival, where it received a 25-minute standing ovation, but has not yet been made available to the wider public. It won a special jury prize at the festival. Speaking then, Abraham said the reporting for the film, which was produced by the UK's Guardian newspaper, had been "rigorous" and that efforts to discredit it were "attempts to not face reality".

"It's a war that has principally been killing civilians. And I think our film is showing that this is not some mistake. It's not an accident. It's something very, very systemic. And this should have been apparent to everyone, I think, from the start. But we are showing it from the inside, with insider testimony," he told the Associated Press in an interview.

The IDF, after initially saying it "categorically rejects [the] allegations", later issued a new statement via its spokesperson Brig-Gen Effie Defrin, saying: "The film 'Naza' has not yet been released in full. However, based on what can be seen in promotional material, it presents a series of serious and false allegations regarding the IDF and its personnel.

"To enable a substantive, professional, and fact-based discussion, rather than one based on misleading portrayals, I invite the filmmakers to allow IDF representatives to view the film in full so that we can address each of the allegations it raises on merits."

Other Israeli politicians have criticised the documentary, including former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who called it a "horrific blood libel against our sons and daughters", and former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman, who described the directors as "haters of Israel".

But more than 700 members of the film industry signed a petition in support of the filmmakers, saying they were being subjected to a "campaign of incitement and vilification". Speaking to Israel's N12 channel, Israeli actor and screenwriter Shlomi Elkabetz said: "These are questions [raised in the film] that must be examined, not silenced."
